headings: 5.9 THE POTENTIAL ENERGY OF A SPRING
pages.page_summary: The page concludes a previous problem regarding a pendulum, calculating the ratio of kinetic energies at points B and C (3:1) and describing the projectile motion if the string is cut at point C. It then introduces Section 5.9, 'The Potential Energy of a Spring.' The text defines the spring force as a conservative variable force, introduces Hooke's Law ($F_s = -kx$), and defines the spring constant $k$. It derives the work done by the spring force ($W_s = -kx_m^2/2$) using integration and by calculating the area of the triangle in the force-displacement graph.
knowledge_points: The ratio of kinetic energies at points B and C is 3:1.
At point C, the string becomes slack and the velocity of the bob is horizontal and to the left.
If the string is cut at point C, the bob executes projectile motion with horizontal projection.
The spring force is an example of a variable force which is conservative.
In an ideal spring, the spring force $F_s$ is proportional to displacement $x$ from the equilibrium position.
Hooke's law is mathematically stated as $F_s = -kx$.
The constant $k$ is the spring constant, with units of N m⁻¹.
A spring is stiff if $k$ is large and soft if $k$ is small.
The work done by the spring force for an extension $x_m$ is $W_s = -kx_m^2/2$.
The work done by the spring force can be obtained by considering the area of the triangle in the $F_s$ vs $x$ plot.
The work done by the external pulling force $F$ is positive since it overcomes the spring force.
For a compressed spring with displacement $x_c$ (< 0), the spring force does work $W_s = -kx_c^2/2$.

embedded_text.visual_description: Figure 5.7(a): A block attached to a spring on a horizontal surface at equilibrium.
Figure 5.7(b): A block attached to a stretched spring.
Figure 5.7(c): A block attached to a compressed spring.
Figure 5.7(d): A graph of spring force Fs versus displacement x.

visuals.description: Figure 5.7: A four-part illustration showing a block attached to a spring on a horizontal surface. Parts (a), (b), and (c) depict the spring at equilibrium, stretched, and compressed respectively, with force vectors and displacement labels. Part (d) is a graph of spring force ($F_s$) versus displacement ($x$), showing a linear relationship with a negative slope and a shaded triangle representing work done.
visuals.educational_role: Illustrates the direction of spring force relative to displacement for stretched and compressed states, and visualizes the work done by the spring force as the area under the force-displacement curve.
